title: Delivering a message between two connected users
description: Because connections are stateful, the sender's server has to discover which server holds the recipient's socket. That registry lookup and the inter-server hop are the price of a push-based design.

steps.text: Alice sends over her existing WebSocket. No connection setup — that cost was paid once, when she opened the app.
The server persists the message first and assigns it a server-side ordering ID. Persisting before delivering is what makes the message survive a crash mid-delivery.
It asks the registry which server holds Bob's connection. This lookup exists only because connections are stateful — the tier cannot be load-balanced like a stateless one.
The message is forwarded to server B over an internal hop.
Server B writes it to Bob's socket. Bob's device acknowledges and advances its cursor.
Identical up to here: the message is stored regardless of whether anyone can receive it right now.
The registry has no live entry for Bob — either he disconnected cleanly, or his heartbeat TTL expired after his phone lost signal. Both look the same, which is the point of using a TTL.
Nothing more happens. There is no separate offline queue: the message is already durable in the conversation, and a mobile push notification is triggered as a side channel.
When Bob reconnects, his device sends its last-seen cursor and pulls everything after it. The same mechanism handles a two-second blip and a two-week absence.
